sheet-2.description: The north-western blocks of Egg Harbor City's grid, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part runs from New York Avenue at the top to London Avenue at the bottom and from Atlantic Avenue, the 200-foot avenue along the railroad at the left edge (only its inner side is drawn), across White Horse Pike, lettered also Agassiz Avenue, to the middle of the next blocks toward Arago Avenue. First, Second and Third Terraces divide the long blocks between the avenues. The blocks next to Atlantic Avenue hold the town's small industries: Harrison G. Dyar's machine shop for piston rings, idle, with a second building left unfinished in 1922; the idle plant of the Atlantic County Electric Company with its reservoir or spray pond; the Hamilton Shoe Company's McKay shoe factory; the Atlantic Cut Glass Works served by a railroad siding; and Julius Einsiedel and Son's Egg Harbor City Pottery with its kiln, drying racks and brick press. A concrete-block repair shop with an office and showroom stands on White Horse Pike at Second Terrace. The rest of the sheet is frame dwellings on narrow lots, many of them still vacant. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches and hydrants are marked in the streets.
notes: White Horse Pike is lettered also as Agassiz Avenue; the index lists Agassiz Avenue under White Horse Pike.
Atlantic Avenue is drawn 200 ft wide with only its inner edge on the sheet; the modern Atlantic Avenue roadway and parcel gap do not match the old centreline, so it was not used for control.
The New York Avenue junction with White Horse Pike in OpenStreetMap lies north of the drawn street and was not used.
Placed by three points along White Horse Pike only (helmert); London Avenue / White Horse Pike was hand-picked from the north edge of London Avenue.

New York to London Avenues, Atlantic Avenue (left edge, inner side only) to White Horse Pike (Agassiz Av) and beyond; electric plant, shoe factory, cut glass works, pottery. One part. 50 ft. Helmert on White Horse Pike only.

sheet-3.description: A residential district in the north of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between New York Avenue at the top and London Avenue at the bottom, divided by Norfolk and Washington Avenues and by First, Second and Third Terraces, and is crossed by Arago Avenue in the middle; Beethoven Avenue runs along the right edge with only its near side drawn, the far side belonging to sheet 4. The blocks are cut into long narrow lots, a large share of them still vacant. The buildings are almost all frame dwellings of one to two and a half storeys with coops, hen houses and small sheds behind them. The Mount Zion Primitive Baptist Church stands on Norfolk Avenue near Beethoven Avenue, and an unfinished pastor's house, its construction suspended, on Norfolk Avenue west of Arago. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked along the avenues and terraces.
notes: Arago and Beethoven are lettered as avenues; today they are Arago Street and Beethoven Street.
Beethoven Street is drawn on its west side only; its junctions were hand-picked as the drawn edge plus 25 ft, because the detector paired the edge with a lot line 40 ft inside the block.
New York Avenue in OpenStreetMap lies about 30 m north of the drawn street at Arago and Beethoven; its junctions were not used.
Norfolk Avenue is drawn about 13 ft out of parallel with Washington Avenue across the sheet.
New York to London Avenues, Arago Avenue in the middle, Beethoven Avenue at the right edge (west side only). Residential. One part. 50 ft.

sheet-4.description: A thinly built residential district in the north of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between New York Avenue at the top and London Avenue at the bottom, divided by Norfolk and Washington Avenues and by First, Second and Third Terraces, and is crossed by Buerger Avenue; Beethoven Avenue runs along the left edge with only its east side drawn, and the right edge cuts the next blocks toward Campe Street. Most lots are laid out but vacant. The scattered buildings are frame dwellings with coops, hen houses and storage sheds. Two churches stand on Washington Avenue: St. John's Reformed Church, with two towers, between Beethoven and Buerger Avenues, and Heard's A.M.E. Church at Second Terrace near Buerger Avenue. Six-inch and eight-inch water pipes and hydrants are marked along the terraces and Beethoven Avenue.
notes: Beethoven and Buerger are lettered as avenues; today they are Beethoven Street and Buerger Street.
Buerger Avenue is drawn 48.4 ft wide against a 73 ft parcel gap today; street_widths is set to the drawn width.
New York Avenue in OpenStreetMap lies about 28 m north of the drawn street; its junctions were not used.
Four of the five control points were hand-picked from the drawn street edges; the detector paired edges with lot lines and the scale bar.
New York to London Avenues, Beethoven Avenue at left edge (east side only), Buerger Avenue. Thinly built; St. John's Reformed and Heard's A.M.E. churches. One part. 50 ft.

sheet-5.description: The railroad strip on the west side of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part runs from Washington Avenue at the top to Philadelphia Avenue at the bottom, between the Philadelphia and Reading Railway (Atlantic City Division) near the left edge and the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania Railroad) in the middle of the 200-foot Atlantic Avenue at the right; the city limits follow both lines. A narrow strip west of the Reading line shows Broad Street, not opened north of Mays Landing County Boulevard, and the west end of Liverpool Avenue. Between the railroads lie the blocks of Third, Fourth and Fifth Terraces and London and Liverpool Avenues, given largely to lumber and industry: the Egg Harbor Coal and Lumber Company yard with sash and lumber sheds, a carpenter shop and coal bins on a curving siding; S. Winterbottom's factory for wood, bone and celluloid knife handles; a Standard Oil Company tank station; and H. Bozarth's lumber yard with its office and lumber, tool and wagon shed on Philadelphia Avenue. A garage for 55 cars stands at Fifth Terrace near Atlantic Avenue. The Reading line has a passenger station, freight house and waiting room, and the Pennsylvania line its railroad depot with ticket office and waiting room at Philadelphia Avenue. A few frame dwellings fill the rest.
notes: Mays Landing County Boulevard is County Boulevard in OpenStreetMap.
The Philadelphia and Reading line through the sheet has been removed; the West Jersey and Seashore line is the present Atlantic City Line.
Atlantic Avenue is drawn 200 ft wide around the railroad; its modern roadways and parcel gaps do not match the drawn street lines, so it was not used for control.
Placed by three points only: the Atlantic City Line crossing of Philadelphia Avenue and two hand-picked junctions on Broad Street. Low confidence.

Railroad strip: Washington to Philadelphia Avenues between the P&R Ry (A.C. Div, removed) and the W.J.&S. R.R. in 200 ft Atlantic Avenue; Broad St and Mays Landing County Blvd at left. Lumber yards, knife-handle factory, depots. One part. 50 ft. Weak control (rail crossing plus two Broad St hand picks).

sheet-6.description: The western half of Egg Harbor City's business district, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between London Avenue at the top and Cincinnati Avenue at the bottom, from Atlantic Avenue at the left edge, the 200-foot avenue along the railroad of which only the inner side is drawn, across White Horse Pike (Agassiz Avenue) to the middle of the next blocks toward Arago Avenue. Fourth, Fifth (Kent Place) and Sixth (Dexter Place) Terraces divide the blocks. The northern blocks are dwellings, with the Emanuel Congregational Church on Liverpool Avenue. South of Liverpool Avenue the sheet becomes commercial: the Aurora Hall and Aurora Hotel with bowling alleys, the H. T. Dewey and Sons wine cellars and wine press room, auto repair shops and garages for 12 and 22 cars, the New York Hotel, the Columbia House and American House, a block of apartments, the Fire Department central station, the jail and the post office. On Philadelphia Avenue stand the Sindel and Schiff Company clothing factory, built of concrete block with sprinklers, a Chinese laundry, a bottling works, a photo gallery, tailor, drug and furniture stores, and a newspaper office. The Egg Harbor Coal and Lumber Company's yard, with lumber sheds, a coal pile, a planing and carpenter shop and a curving siding from the railroad, fills the block between Sixth Terrace and Cincinnati Avenue.
notes: White Horse Pike is lettered also as Agassiz Avenue.
Fifth Terrace is also lettered Kent Place and Sixth Terrace Dexter Place; Sixth Terrace keeps the name 6th Terrace in OpenStreetMap.
All control lies along White Horse Pike (helmert); Atlantic Avenue at the left edge was not used. The Cincinnati Avenue junction was hand-picked from the north edge of the avenue.

London to Cincinnati Avenues, Atlantic Avenue (left edge) to White Horse Pike and beyond; business district, hotels, post office, fire station, clothing factory, coal and lumber yard. One part. 50 ft. Helmert on White Horse Pike only.

sheet-7.description: The commercial centre of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between London Avenue at the top and Cincinnati Avenue at the bottom, crossed by Arago Avenue in the middle, and reaches Beethoven Avenue at the right edge, whose far side is left to sheet 8. The street names on the sheet are the avenues London, Liverpool, Philadelphia and Cincinnati, with the narrow Fourth, Fifth (Kent Place) and Sixth (Dexter Place) Terraces between them. The residential blocks toward London and Liverpool Avenues carry mostly frame dwellings with coops and sheds, the German Baptist Church on London Avenue and a few small shops. The two blocks on Philadelphia Avenue, the 100-foot main street, are lined with stores and offices, many of them brick: a bank, an ice cream and bakery shop, Bissig's Hotel, the G.A.R. Hall, a soda water bottling works, plumbers' shops and storage, the Colonial Moving Picture Theatre and the Philadelphia Hotel. On Liverpool Avenue near Beethoven stand Jacob Dey's blacksmith and wheelwright shop and storage of glass. Fire alarm boxes, hydrants and water pipes of 4 to 10 inches are marked along the streets.
notes: Arago and Beethoven are lettered as avenues; today they are Arago Street and Beethoven Street.
Fifth Terrace is also lettered Kent Place and Sixth Terrace Dexter Place.
Beethoven Street is drawn on its west side only; its two junctions used here were hand-picked as the drawn edge plus 25 ft.
London to Cincinnati Avenues, Arago Avenue in the middle, Beethoven Avenue at the right edge (west side only); main business blocks of Philadelphia Avenue. One part. 50 ft. Pilot sheet.

sheet-8.description: The eastern edge of Egg Harbor City's centre, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between London Avenue at the top and Cincinnati Avenue at the bottom, from Beethoven Avenue at the left edge across Buerger Avenue to the middle of the next blocks toward Campe Street, divided by Fourth, Fifth (Kent Place) and Sixth (Dexter Place) Terraces. The blocks north of Philadelphia Avenue are mostly frame dwellings on narrow lots with coops and a few concrete-block outbuildings; the Hotel Atlantic and a bakery stand at Fifth Terrace and Philadelphia Avenue. On Philadelphia Avenue are stores with a lodge room above, the Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church with its Sunday school, and the Egg Harbor City Water Company's standpipe, 100 feet high. Between Sixth Terrace and Cincinnati Avenue stand William Zuefle and Company's works, makers and packers of Atlantic Brand food products, with a steam retort and a can-capping room, and the old fire station of the Fire Department with the council hall above it. Water pipes of 4 to 12 inches, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked in the streets.
notes: Beethoven and Buerger are lettered as avenues; today they are Beethoven Street and Buerger Street.
Both streets are drawn 48.4 ft wide, narrower than the parcel gaps today; street_widths is set to 48 ft.
London to Cincinnati Avenues, Beethoven Avenue (left edge) and Buerger Avenue; Zion Lutheran Church, water company standpipe, Zuefle food products works. One part. 50 ft.

sheet-9-1.description: The south-western edge of Egg Harbor City's centre between its two railroads, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the land from Philadelphia Avenue at the top to Cincinnati Avenue, and along Atlantic Avenue on the right down to Buffalo Avenue, from the double track of the Philadelphia and Reading Railway (Atlantic City Division) at the left edge to the tracks of the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania Railroad System) in the middle of the 200 ft Atlantic Avenue on the right, with the city limits drawn along them. Cape May Avenue, marked not open, cuts diagonally across the block toward Philadelphia Avenue. The blocks between the railroads are industrial: H. H. Bozarth's box mill, saw mill, lumber shed and storage of old machinery, and the yard of Harry R. Rupp, dealer in lime, cement and masons' materials, with brick and cement block making, cement ornamental work, a brick kiln, drying racks and cord wood piles, and Rupp's office for building materials near the railroad. Beside the West Jersey and Seashore tracks are the Pennsylvania Railroad freight house and platform, a section house, a hand car house and a gateman's house. Below Cincinnati Avenue lie the Egg Harbor Coal and Lumber Company's sheds, storage of barrels, shooks and cut glass, a wagon and coal shed, storage for cement and plaster and for barrels and straw, and the tanks of the Crew Levick Oil Company. A siding curves off the main line toward the blocks east of Atlantic Avenue.
notes: Placed from hand-picked railroad crossings only: three on the West Jersey and Seashore tracks (now the Atlantic City Line) and two on the Philadelphia and Reading tracks carried from sheet 16. Medium to low confidence.

The Philadelphia and Reading line through the sheet has been removed; its bed is now Aloe Street, which runs about 12 m east (along the avenues) of the drawn track centre, as measured here and on sheet 16.
Cape May Avenue is marked not open; the modern Cape May Avenue starts further south-west at Aloe Street and does not follow this line.
The Pennsylvania Railroad tracks in Atlantic Avenue are lettered W. J. and S. R. R. (P. R. R. System).

Three parts: 1 main (Philadelphia to Buffalo Avs between the P&R and WJ&S railroads; Bozarth mill, Rupp lime and cement, Egg Harbor Coal & Lumber), placed from rail crossings only (3 on the WJ&S tracks in Atlantic Av, 2 carried from sheet-16 on the old P&R line); 2 Cologne inset ("3 miles S of P.O."), anchored, low confidence; 3 L. N. Renault & Sons champagne works on Bremen Av, unplaced. 50 ft.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: L. N. Renault & Sons champagne works, Bremen Avenue ("2 1/2 miles S.E. of P.O.") (no street junction; needs hand placement from aerial imagery or a modern survey of the winery buildings).

sheet-9-2.description: An inset of the village of Cologne, lettered as located 3 miles south of the Egg Harbor City post office, drawn at 50 feet to an inch inside a heavy frame on sheet 9, with its own north arrow pointing to the upper right as on the main map. It shows Cologne Avenue running across the inset where it crosses the double track of the Philadelphia and Reading Railway (Atlantic City Division), with a siding curving away south-east from the main line toward a warehouse. Beside the tracks stand the Cologne passenger depot north of the avenue and the freight depot with a platform south of it. East of the railroad the Germania Fruit Growers Union and Co-operative Society Ltd. occupies a row of buildings along the siding: a store, storage, a reinforced concrete building for feed and supplies, hay and feed storage, an oil house with a kerosene oil tank and further storage buildings, with a note of a night watchman and approved clock and underwriters' extinguishers. A public school heated by stoves stands on Cologne Avenue to the east, and a single dwelling west of the railroad. The rest of the inset is open land.
notes: Placed by hand from one point, Cologne Avenue at the railroad, with a derived second point; low confidence. The railroad has been removed and its bed is now Aloe Street; the point was moved 12 m south-west of the Aloe Street / Cologne Avenue junction by the offset measured in Egg Harbor City.
Germania Fruit Growers Union and Co-operative Society Ltd. at the Cologne station.

Three parts: 1 main (Philadelphia to Buffalo Avs between the P&R and WJ&S railroads; Bozarth mill, Rupp lime and cement, Egg Harbor Coal & Lumber), placed from rail crossings only (3 on the WJ&S tracks in Atlantic Av, 2 carried from sheet-16 on the old P&R line); 2 Cologne inset ("3 miles S of P.O."), anchored, low confidence; 3 L. N. Renault & Sons champagne works on Bremen Av, unplaced. 50 ft.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: L. N. Renault & Sons champagne works, Bremen Avenue ("2 1/2 miles S.E. of P.O.") (no street junction; needs hand placement from aerial imagery or a modern survey of the winery buildings).

sheet-10.description: The south-western side of Egg Harbor City's centre, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between Cincinnati Avenue at the top and St. Louis Avenue at the bottom, from Atlantic Avenue at the left edge, whose wide right-of-way with the railroad lies mostly off the sheet, across White Horse Pike (lettered Agassiz Avenue) to the middle of the blocks toward Arago Avenue. West of the Pike the sheet is given over to large public and industrial sites. Between Cincinnati and Buffalo Avenues lies the public park with a band stand, and in its corner the Enterprise Gas Company's works, with a generator house, purifying house, coal shed and two gas holders of 25,000 and 51,000 cubic feet. Between Buffalo and Chicago Avenues stand the Liberty Cut Glass Works, the muslin underwear factory of Theo. F. Baulig with a separate cutting room and storage building, and the public school, heated by steam. Between Chicago and St. Louis Avenues are the ball park and the fair grounds inside an iron-clad fence, with a grand stand, dance pavilion, band stand, Granger's building, cattle sheds, a poultry house and an electric transformer house. East of the Pike are blocks of frame dwellings divided by Seventh, Eighth and Ninth Terraces. A narrow watercourse, coloured blue, runs along Eighth Terrace and on west of the Pike behind the glass works. Water pipes and hydrants are marked in the streets.
notes: White Horse Pike is lettered with its old name, Agassiz Avenue, in brackets.
Chicago Avenue between the school block and White Horse Pike is marked not opened.
Placed by a helmert transformation from four junctions along White Horse Pike; Atlantic Avenue gives no usable control (its modern roadways and parcel gaps do not match the drawn street lines).
The park is lettered "Puplic Park" on the sheet.
Cincinnati to St. Louis Avs, Atlantic Av to east of White Horse Pike; park, gas works, Liberty Cut Glass Works, Baulig factory, school, fair grounds. One part. 50 ft. Helmert on White Horse Pike.

sheet-11.description: A residential district in the centre of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between Cincinnati Avenue at the top and St. Louis Avenue at the bottom, from the middle of the blocks east of White Horse Pike across Arago Avenue to Beethoven Avenue, which runs along the right edge with only its near side drawn. The blocks are divided by Seventh, Eighth and Ninth Terraces; a narrow watercourse, coloured blue, runs down the middle of Eighth Terrace. Most lots are long and narrow and hold frame dwellings with sheds, coops and outbuildings, and many lots, especially between Chicago and St. Louis Avenues, are still empty. Small industries are scattered among the houses: the Drapar Mills with 60 sewing machines and a steam-heated cutting room on Seventh Terrace, Germania Hall with storage, a chewing tobacco factory and a cigar factory west of Arago Avenue, carpet weaving, Henderson and Company's printing shop at Arago Avenue and Eighth Terrace, and tailor shops including that of Altman and Richter and one of G. Blankner. W. J. Thomas, florist, has a hot house on Seventh Terrace. Water pipes of 4 and 8 inches, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked in the streets.
notes: Arago and Beethoven are lettered as avenues; today they are Arago Street and Beethoven Street.
Beethoven Avenue is cut by the right edge; its junctions were placed from the drawn west edge plus half the 48 ft drawn width.
The terraces are not in the modern street data and give no control.
Cincinnati to St. Louis Avs, Arago to Beethoven (Beethoven cut by the edge). One part. 50 ft.

sheet-12.description: A residential district east of the centre of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 50 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between Cincinnati Avenue at the top and St. Louis Avenue at the bottom, from Beethoven Avenue at the left edge across Buerger Avenue to the middle of the blocks toward Campe Street. The blocks are divided by Seventh, Eighth and Ninth Terraces. A narrow watercourse, coloured blue, runs down Eighth Terrace and east of Buerger Avenue turns diagonally across the block to Buffalo Avenue, where it passes under a small building and continues along the avenue toward sheet 15. The lots hold frame dwellings with sheds and coops, many of them still empty. Among them are a plumbing and heating shop at Cincinnati Avenue, the printing works of the Tribune Publishing Company with electric light and a gas engine at Buerger Avenue and Seventh Terrace, an insurance office on Buerger Avenue, Chas. Blattner's tailor shop on Eighth Terrace, a clothing factory near Beethoven Avenue and Ninth Terrace, and a carpet shop. On Ninth Terrace east of Buerger stand the concrete old jail, a building for the Department of Public Works wagons and the fire department hose cart, with a fire siren. Water pipes of 4 to 8 inches, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked in the streets.
notes: Beethoven and Buerger are lettered as avenues; today they are Beethoven Street and Buerger Street.
Buerger Avenue / St. Louis Avenue was hand-picked: the detector paired the north edge of St. Louis Avenue with the scale bar.
The terraces are not in the modern street data and give no control.
Cincinnati to St. Louis Avs, Beethoven to east of Buerger; Buerger / St. Louis hand-picked (scale bar in the street). One part. 50 ft.

sheet-13-1.description: The south-western end of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 100 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between St. Louis Avenue at the top and Baltimore Avenue at the bottom, from Atlantic Avenue at the left edge, with a note giving 91 ft to the railroad, across White Horse Pike (lettered Agassiz Avenue) and Arago Avenue to Beethoven Avenue at the right edge. Between the avenues run Tenth to Fifteenth Terraces. The district is laid out in long rows of narrow lots, nearly all of them empty: frame dwellings stand mainly along St. Louis Avenue and near White Horse Pike, with sheds, coops and garages behind them. The few other buildings are a concrete-block garage for eight cars with an iron truss roof at White Horse Pike and Tenth Terrace, a concrete-block greenhouse near Havana Avenue, the Moravian Church near Beethoven Avenue and Tenth Terrace, kennels, open coops and a pigeon house between San Francisco and New Orleans Avenues. Water pipes run in White Horse Pike, Tenth and Eleventh Terraces and Beethoven Avenue, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The lower right corner of the sheet holds a separate inset (part 2).
notes: White Horse Pike is lettered with its old name, Agassiz Avenue, in brackets; Arago and Beethoven are lettered as avenues and are Arago Street and Beethoven Street today.
Antwerp Avenue / Arago Street (6.1 m) and Beethoven Street / Boston Avenue (7.1 m) were detected but rejected by the fit.
Moravian Church near Beethoven Avenue.

Two parts: 1 St. Louis to Baltimore Avs, Atlantic to Beethoven; 2 inset Baltimore to Bremen Avs east of Atlantic (Velvet Soap Products, Singer Park), anchored, low confidence; it draws Bremen about 265 ft closer to Baltimore than today. 100 ft.

sheet-13-2.description: A small inset in the lower right corner of sheet 13, framed by a heavy line and drawn at 100 feet to an inch in the same orientation as the main map, north to the upper right. It shows the block on the east side of Atlantic Avenue between Baltimore Avenue at the top and Bremen Avenue at the bottom, just south of the main map. Atlantic Avenue is lettered 200 ft wide, with a note giving 91 ft from its east side to the railroad; Baltimore Avenue is 80 ft and Bremen Avenue 70 ft wide, and Bremen Avenue is marked as the city limits. At the corner of Atlantic and Baltimore Avenues stands the soap factory of Velvet Soap Products Inc., a two-storey building with a concrete floor, steam heat and electric light, with a watchman but no clock. The rest of the block and the land beyond it are lettered Singer Park and are otherwise empty. A further block south of Bremen Avenue is outlined but blank.
notes: Placed by hand: one point where Baltimore Avenue meets the railroad (91 ft west of the drawn east side of Atlantic Avenue) and a derived point 300 ft along Baltimore Avenue at the scale and rotation of part 1. Low confidence.

The inset draws Bremen Avenue about 405 ft (centre to centre) south of Baltimore Avenue; modern Bremen Avenue is about 670 ft away, so the Bremen Avenue side of the inset lies about 80 m short of the modern street.
Bremen Avenue is marked as the city limits.

sheet-14-1.description: The south-eastern residential side of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 100 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between Chicago Avenue at the top and San Francisco Avenue at the bottom, from Beethoven Avenue at the left edge across Buerger and Campe Avenues to Claudius Avenue and the start of the next blocks at the right edge; a heavy double line below San Francisco Avenue separates it from part 2. Ninth to Twelfth Terraces divide the blocks. The upper left corner, west of Buerger Avenue above St. Louis Avenue, is left blank (it is on sheet 12). Along St. Louis Avenue the lots are fairly well built with frame dwellings and stores, among them a hotel between Buerger and Campe Avenues and the town jail near Beethoven Avenue; toward San Francisco Avenue most lots are empty, with a few dwellings, coops and a greenhouse. Between Campe and Claudius Avenues on Ninth Terrace stand the Catholic church, heated by hot air and lit by electricity, with a 75 ft tower, and its parochial school; there is also a tailor shop on St. Louis Avenue. Water pipes of 4 to 8 inches run in St. Louis Avenue and the terraces, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes.
notes: Beethoven, Buerger, Campe and Claudius are lettered as avenues; today they are streets of the same names.
Catholic church with a 75 ft tower and parochial school on Ninth Terrace.
Two parts: 1 Chicago to San Francisco Avs, Beethoven to Claudius (fits 3.95 px/ft, 1.3% under the other 100 ft sheets); 2 Hamburg Av (city limits) to New York Av, Bloch Go-Cart Co, helmert. 100 ft.

sheet-14-2.description: The north-western edge of Egg Harbor City, below a heavy double line on sheet 14, drawn at 100 feet to an inch in the same orientation as part 1, north to the upper right. It covers the strip between Hamburg Avenue, marked as the city limits, and New York Avenue at the bottom, from Atlantic Avenue at the left edge, lettered 200 ft wide and not open, with a note giving 91 ft to the railroad, across White Horse Pike (lettered Agassiz Avenue) and Arago Avenue to Beethoven Avenue at the right edge, together with a row of lots on the far side of Hamburg Avenue. The three large blocks are unsubdivided and numbered 1G, 2G and 3G. In the first, at Atlantic and New York Avenues, stand the works of the Bloch Go-Cart Company, makers of go-carts and reed furniture, with finishing, upholstering and shipping, reed working and woodworking rooms and two warehouses, heated by steam and powered by electricity. At White Horse Pike and Hamburg Avenue are a concrete-floored garage for 13 cars and a hotel; the middle block is a poultry farm with coops, and the block toward Beethoven Avenue holds a few dwellings and coops. A work shop stands across Hamburg Avenue.
notes: Hamburg Avenue is drawn as the city limits.
Atlantic Avenue is marked not open here.
Placed by a helmert transformation from three junctions along Hamburg Avenue; New York Avenue was not used because its modern line lies about 28 m from the drawn street (see sheets 2 to 4).
White Horse Pike is lettered with its old name, Agassiz Avenue.
Two parts: 1 Chicago to San Francisco Avs, Beethoven to Claudius (fits 3.95 px/ft, 1.3% under the other 100 ft sheets); 2 Hamburg Av (city limits) to New York Av, Bloch Go-Cart Co, helmert. 100 ft.

sheet-15.description: The north-eastern side of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 100 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The part covers the blocks between Washington Avenue at the top and Chicago Avenue at the bottom, from the blocks west of Campe Avenue across Campe and Claudius Avenues to Diesterweg Avenue and the half blocks beyond it, divided by Third to Eighth Terraces. Most lots are still empty; frame dwellings are scattered thinly, closer together toward Campe Avenue. A stream, coloured blue, enters from Washington Avenue and runs south to London Avenue, where it feeds a serpentine channel ending at a wood bridge on Fourth Terrace. Beside it lies the Neutral Water Health Resort, with a 90 ft lookout tower, two round pavilions ringed by water, a building of private rooms with glass-covered grass beds, a doctor's office with rooms above, an old power house and bath houses. On Claudius Avenue at Fourth Terrace stands the pumping station of the Egg Harbor City Water Company. At Campe Avenue and Fifth Terrace is the Atz Beverage Company's brewery, with a brew house, engine room, racking room and concrete cold storage, noted as not in operation, padlocked and admittance refused. Other buildings are the Philadelphia Avenue public school, the Shiloh Baptist Church on Philadelphia Avenue, a Baptist church lettered "Colored" on Cincinnati Avenue, a tailor shop and a few stores. Water pipes, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked.
notes: Campe, Claudius and Diesterweg are lettered as avenues; today they are Campe Street, Claudius Street and Diesterweg Street.
Four junctions on Claudius and Diesterweg south of Liverpool Avenue were excluded: the detector read one street edge as the other and placed them 30 to 45 ft off; 14 junctions remain.
Atz Beverage Company brewery marked not in operation, padlocked.

Washington to Chicago Avs, Campe to Diesterweg; Neutral Water Health Resort, water company pumping station, Atz brewery. Four Claudius/Diesterweg junctions excluded (detector placed them on the wrong side of a single edge). One part. 100 ft.

sheet-16.description: Egg Harbor City Manor, a planned subdivision west of the railroad on the western side of Egg Harbor City, drawn at 100 feet to an inch on a sheet turned so that north points to the upper right. The name is spread in large letters diagonally across the whole sheet. The part covers the grid between an unnamed street at the top and Cincinnati Avenue at the bottom: Wilson Avenue, Mays Landing County Boulevard, Liverpool Avenue, Philadelphia Avenue and Sixth Terrace run across it, and the cross streets are Tyree, Baker, Pittsburg, Detroit, Williams, Cleveland and Broad north of the County Boulevard and Irving, Hamilton, Grand, Fairmont, Empire, Dekalb, Cleveland and Broad south of it, offset from one another. South of Philadelphia Avenue the cross streets are lettered not named and not opened. The blocks are numbered 60 to 143 and cut into very narrow lots, almost all of them empty; only a handful of frame dwellings, coops and hen houses stand among them, mostly near Cleveland and Broad and south of Philadelphia Avenue. The only public building is St. Paul's C.M.E. Church near Grand and Fairmont Avenues, heated by stove and lit by electricity. Along the right edge runs the Philadelphia and Reading Railway (Atlantic City Division), and beyond it a narrow strip lists the ends of the avenues and terraces of the town on the far side (New York Avenue to Liverpool Avenue).
notes: Mays Landing County Boulevard is County Boulevard today; Dekalb and Broad are Dekalb Street and Broad Street.
Tyree, Baker, Detroit, Williams, Irving, Hamilton, Grand and Wilson are not in the modern street data for the Manor (an Irving Street elsewhere in the town is not this one).
The railroad is lettered P. & R. Ry. (A.C. Div'n), now the New Jersey Transit Atlantic City Line.
Dekalb / Philadelphia and Cleveland / Philadelphia were excluded: the scale bar is drawn in Philadelphia Avenue there and was paired with the street edge.
Control is from the County Boulevard, Liverpool and Philadelphia rows only; the blocks above the County Boulevard have no control of their own.

Egg Harbor City Manor west of the railroads, Wilson to Cincinnati Avs, Tyree/Irving to Broad; St. Paul's C.M.E. Church; scale bar junction excluded and hand-picked. The old P&R railbed is now Aloe Street, about 12 m NE of the drawn track centre. One part. 100 ft (confirmed).
